summary: Specifies the Mail Transfer Protocol, an early way for hosts to deliver mail to one another. It was a step toward the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol that came later. Replaced by RFC 780.

eli5.summary: This is the rulebook computers once used to hand letters to each other, like mail carriers passing bags at a depot. A later version replaced it.

subtitle: A simple way to transfer messages between network computers, the predecessor to SMTP.

tldr.problem: Early networks needed a way to reliably send mail messages from one computer to another, with support for multiple recipients and error handling.
tldr.mechanism: MTP establishes a control connection between a sender and receiver using TELNET, exchanges commands and replies with numeric codes, and transfers mail as a stream of text, with commands like MAIL, MRSQ, and MRCP to handle single and multiple recipients.
tldr.outcome: MTP enabled mail transfer on the ARPANET and served as a prototype for later mail protocols. It was replaced by RFC 780, which became the basis for the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP).

today: MTP is obsolete, replaced by RFC 780, which was replaced by RFC 821 (SMTP). It survives in history as the first practical mail transfer protocol for the ARPANET.

sections.title: Introduction and Model
sections.content:
Mail Transfer Protocol (MTP) is a way for one computer to reliably send messages to another over the ARPANET. It builds on ideas from the File Transfer Protocol and uses the TELNET protocol for communication.

The basic model has two sides: a sender-MTP process that initiates the connection and a receiver-MTP process that listens on a known port. They establish a control connection following TELNET rules, then exchange commands and replies to transfer mail.
sections.eli5: Two mail carriers meet over a phone line. One picks up, they agree on which messages to send and in what order, then the message goes through.

sections.title: Commands and Replies
sections.content:
The sender-MTP sends commands like MAIL FROM:<sender@host> TO:<recipient@host> to transfer a message, or MRSQ to set a scheme for multiple recipients. The receiver replies with three-digit codes where the first digit shows success (2xx), failure (4xx or 5xx), or an incomplete state (3xx) needing more information.

For multiple recipients, the sender can use the recipients-first scheme (MRSQ R) to list all recipients first then send the text once, or the text-first scheme (MRSQ T) to send the text first then specify recipients. This flexibility helps both simple and complex mail systems.
sections.eli5: The sender says 'I have mail from Alice for Bob', the receiver says 'OK, send it' (code 354), then the sender transmits the message, and the receiver says 'Got it' (code 250).

sections.title: Mail Format and Representation
sections.content:
All mail is represented in NVT-ASCII, the standard Network Virtual Terminal text format, regardless of how the sending or receiving computer normally stores text. The sender converts from its internal format to NVT-ASCII, transmits it, and the receiver converts it back. Lines are terminated with CRLF (carriage return and line feed).

Mail itself is treated as a continuous stream of octets with no internal structure. The message text ends when the sender sends a line containing just a period, signaled as CRLF.CRLF. This simple structure makes the protocol easy to implement on different systems.
sections.eli5: No matter if one computer uses one text format and another uses a different one, MTP converts everything to a standard format everyone understands, like translating to a common language.

sections.title: Status
sections.content: RFC 780 superseded MTP, which itself was a step toward the widely used SMTP protocol. MTP is now considered obsolete and is of historical interest only as an early mail protocol design.
sections.eli5: MTP was the first try at a mail protocol. It worked well enough to teach people what a mail protocol should do, and later versions learned from it and became much better.
